prompt: What does a workload send to Google's Security Token Service in the exchange?
hint: Something it already holds from outside.

choices.text: A service account key it downloaded once
choices.why: The whole point of federation is that no key exists.

choices.text: Its outside provider's signed token
choices.why: Right. STS checks it against the pool's provider and returns a federated token.

choices.text: The password of the GitHub account that started the job
choices.why: Passwords never cross. The job's signed token is what is presented.

choices.text: A Google access token from the night before
choices.why: A Google token is what it is trying to get, and yesterday's has expired.

prompt: What does `attribute.repository = assertion.repository` in a provider's mapping do?
hint: It turns a claim into something IAM can select by.

choices.text: Refuses tokens from other repositories
choices.why: Refusing is the condition's job. A mapping only names things.

choices.text: Creates a service account named after the repository
choices.why: No account is created; attributes are labels on federated identities.

choices.text: Sends the repository's code to Google
choices.why: Only the token's claims cross, never code.

choices.text: Names the token's repository claim as an attribute
choices.why: Right. A `principalSet://` can then pick every identity with a given repository.

prompt: A provider trusts GitHub's issuer and has no attribute condition. Why is that dangerous?
hint: Whose tokens does that issuer sign?

choices.text: Strangers' tokens pass too
choices.why: Right. Only whatever roles happen to match would stand between a stranger's workflow and your project.

choices.text: GitHub's tokens last a week without a condition
choices.why: Their life is minutes either way. The danger is whose tokens are accepted.

choices.text: The exchange then skips the signature check
choices.why: The signature is checked regardless. A stranger's token is signed perfectly well.

choices.text: The pool stops working after thirty days
choices.why: Pools do not expire. The issue is who gets in.

prompt: Put the steps of the exchange in order.
items: the outside provider signs a token for the job
STS checks it and returns a federated token
IAM Credentials trades it for the service account's token
trap: Putting IAM Credentials before STS is the slip: impersonating needs a Google credential, and the federated token is the first one the job has.

choices.text: Pool ids may not be lowercase
choices.why: They must be lowercase. The length is the problem.

choices.text: `ci` is reserved by Google
choices.why: Nothing is reserved; `ci-pool` was accepted a moment later.

choices.text: It is shorter than four characters
choices.why: Right. A pool id takes four to thirty-two.

choices.text: A pool needs a provider in the same file
choices.why: A pool alone is valid; the id is what was refused.

prompt: Which role lets identities from a pool act as the deployer service account?
hint: Not the Token Creator of lesson 8.

choices.text: `roles/owner` on the project
choices.why: Far too much, and it does not mention the deployer at all.

choices.text: `roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin`
choices.why: That manages keys, which federation exists to avoid.

choices.text: `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser`, on the deployer
choices.why: Right. It is granted on the account, to the pool's set of identities.

choices.text: `roles/viewer` on the pool
choices.why: Viewer reads the pool; it lets nobody act as anything.

prompt: The grant names `principalSet://.../attribute.repository/example/planner`. Which jobs can act as the deployer?
hint: The set is chosen by repository alone.

choices.text: Any job of that repository, whatever its branch
choices.why: Right. A pull request's branch matches too; restricting to main needs a stricter condition or grant.

choices.text: Only jobs on `main`
choices.why: Nothing in that set mentions a branch. That was the missing lock.

choices.text: Any job in the `example` organisation
choices.why: The condition admits the organisation; the grant narrows it to one repository.

choices.text: No job, until a key is added
choices.why: No key is ever needed; the federated token is enough.

prompt: How many locks stand between a stranger's GitHub workflow and the deployer in `pool.tf`?
hint: One on the provider, one on the account.

choices.text: One: the issuer, since GitHub signs the token
choices.why: GitHub signs strangers' tokens too. The issuer is not a lock.

choices.text: None: anybody on GitHub can act as the deployer
choices.why: The condition and the grant both have to match, and a stranger's token matches neither.

choices.text: Three: issuer, condition and a key
choices.why: There is no key in federation.

choices.text: Two, one on each side
choices.why: Right. The condition admits only `example`, and the grant names only `example/planner`.

prompt: What is the largest number of characters a workload identity pool id may have?
Why can a credential configuration file sit in a repository when a key file cannot?

choices.text: It is encrypted by gcloud
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted; the file is plain JSON with no secret in it.

choices.text: It says where the token is, not what it is
choices.why: Right. It holds no secret; the token appears only when the workload runs.

choices.text: It expires after an hour
choices.why: The tokens expire; the file is configuration and does not.

choices.text: Google deletes it if it is published
choices.why: Nobody deletes it, and there would be nothing to fear if it were read.

prompt: Match each field of `credentials.json` to the step it describes.

pairs.right: where the outside token will be
the pool and provider presented to
the trade for the deployer's token

right_distractors: the private key of the account

prompt: In the lab, `gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create-cred-config` succeeded though the pool does not exist. Why?

choices.text: It asks Google nothing
choices.why: Right. The file only records names and addresses; checking them happens at exchange time.

choices.text: The emulator answered for the pool
choices.why: The emulator is Pub/Sub only.

choices.text: Google creates the pool on first use
choices.why: Nothing creates the pool except a request to IAM, which was never sent.

choices.text: The placeholder token was accepted for this one command
choices.why: No token was sent; the command is local.

prompt: STS answered `invalid_target` to the lab's exchange. What was it refusing?
hint: It never got as far as the token.

choices.text: The text `not-a-real-token`, as a bad signature
choices.why: With a real pool, that would be the refusal. Here the audience failed first.

choices.text: The missing Google credential
choices.why: STS is called without one; it issues the first.

choices.text: The audience: no such pool was found
choices.why: Right. The pool in a made-up project could not be found, so the token was never read.

choices.text: The condition on `repository_owner`
choices.why: The condition is read only once a pool and a valid token are found.

prompt: A credential configuration file for federation says `type: ___`, where a key file would say `service_account`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: A workflow in `example/planner` deploys from `main`, and outside contributors open pull requests from their own branches of the same repository. What makes sure only `main` can act as the deployer?
hint: The repository alone matches every branch.

choices.text: The organisation condition already in `pool.tf`
choices.why: It admits every repository of `example`, branches included.

choices.text: Naming the ref in the condition as well
choices.why: Right. A set chosen by repository matches pull request branches too; the ref closes it.

choices.text: A key stored only in `main`'s secrets
choices.why: That brings back the key federation removed.

choices.text: Shortening the token's lifetime to a minute
choices.why: A minute is plenty for a pull request's job to deploy.
